proof_nl: Let R = Q[q,q^{-1}] and let S = {V(q) in Q[q] : gcd(V(q), M(q)) = 1}. By definition, Loc_M = S^{-1}R. Since R is an integral domain and every element of S is nonzero, the canonical map S^{-1}R -> Frac(R) is injective; and Frac(R) = Q(q). So we may regard Loc_M as a subring of Q(q). Now gcd(U(q), M(q)) = 1, so U(q) belongs to S. Therefore U(q) is invertible in Loc_M, and because H(q) is in R, the element H(q)/U(q) belongs to Loc_M. The hypothesis gives the identity U(q)(X(q)-Y(q)) = M(q)H(q) in Q(q). Since U(q) is a nonzero rational function, we may divide by U(q) in Q(q) and obtain X(q)-Y(q) = M(q)·(H(q)/U(q)). The factor H(q)/U(q) lies in Loc_M, so the right-hand side belongs to M(q)·Loc_M. Hence X(q)-Y(q) belongs to M(q)·Loc_M. By the definition of congruence modulo M(q), this is exactly X(q) ≡ Y(q) mod M(q).
solver_summary: Because gcd(U,M)=1, the localization Loc_M inverts U. Thus H/U is an element of Loc_M, and the given identity rewrites as X-Y = M(H/U). Therefore X-Y lies in the ideal M·Loc_M, which is exactly the desired congruence.

This directly proves X-Y ∈ M·Loc_M, which is exactly the stated congruence. The argument matches the lemma sketch and the intended assembly role.
